oil.summary: Crude sold off sharply on Wednesday as diplomatic progress on Hormuz corridor talks undercut the geopolitical risk premium that had been supporting prices. Brent shed 2.38% to $86.47 and WTI fell 0.66% to $81.82, extending a brutal weekly decline of 5.6% and 4.7% respectively. The steepest move was in RBOB gasoline, down 10% on the day and 12% on the month, signalling demand-side softness alongside supply relief. Partially offsetting the bearish tone: Ukrainian drone campaigns knocked Russian petroleum product output 19.3%, Rystad cut its Russia crude forecast to 8.95 mb/d, and India's Russian imports eased from record highs as export infrastructure remains disrupted. Aramco is building ship-to-ship transfer workarounds to keep Saudi barrels flowing to Asia, a sign logistics stress is not fully resolved. EIA data showed U.S. crude stocks barely moved (+100k bbl) while gasoline inventories fell.
drivers: Iran-Oman maritime corridor talks signal partial Hormuz reopening, deflating the geopolitical risk premium in Brent and WTI
Ukrainian drone strikes cut Russian petroleum product output 19.3% and prompted Rystad to lower Russia 2026 crude forecast to 8.95 mb/d
RBOB gasoline collapsed 10% on the day, pointing to demand weakness compounding supply-side re-rating

gas.summary: Henry Hub jumped 4.69% to $2.90/MMBtu, extending a month-long rally of nearly 9%, while TTF slipped 0.62% to €66.18/MWh but remains 14.6% higher on the month. The divergence reflects distinct regional dynamics: U.S. gas is catching a bid on export demand expectations and domestic tightness, while European spot prices are already pricing in serious supply stress. Six months of Iran-war disruption have cost Qatar an estimated $24 billion as LNG exports collapsed 96%, removing a critical supply source for European importers. The Netherlands has formally warned it will miss winter storage targets, and UK energy regulators are expected to raise household bills to a three-year high. European policymakers are increasingly focused on natural gas as the primary inflation risk, with bond markets beginning to price the scenario accordingly. Supply diversification remains limited near-term.
drivers: Qatar's LNG exports down 96% since the Iran war began, costing $24 billion and stranding Europe's key swing supply source
Netherlands confirms it will miss winter gas storage fill targets, raising draw-down and price spike risk heading into Q4
Henry Hub +4.69% on the day as U.S. gas catches a bid; European inflation fears increasingly centred on gas rather than oil

power.summary: The power and carbon complex faces a compounding stress backdrop with limited bullish price relief visible today. EU EUAs dipped 1.20% to $78.61, a modest pullback within an otherwise range-bound monthly move of +0.80%, suggesting the carbon market is not yet fully pricing the broader energy shock. TTF, the key marginal cost signal for gas-fired generation, remains 14.6% higher on the month despite today's small retreat. European heatwaves are simultaneously pressuring nuclear output — cooling water constraints cited — at precisely the moment gas supply is most strained from Hormuz disruption. Marco Rubio's statement that there will be 'no further strikes on Iran for now' may reduce tail-risk slightly, but tightened U.S. sanctions on Iranian oil exports maintain the structural supply squeeze. News flow for this sector today is relatively thin beyond these macro overlays.
drivers: European heatwaves stressing nuclear capacity at the same time gas supply remains severely curtailed by the Iran-war disruption
TTF +14.6% month-on-month keeps marginal generation costs elevated, pressuring power prices even as EUAs trade sideways
Rubio's pause on Iran strikes offers modest geopolitical relief, but new U.S. sanctions on Iranian oil exports sustain the underlying supply shock
